title: Copyleft or permissive?
description: Sort licences and licence descriptions by what they demand when someone passes the work on.

items.why: The GPL is the best-known copyleft licence: anyone who passes on the software or a changed version must give the same freedoms and the source.
The BSD licences ask mostly that the copyright notice stays. A company may take BSD code and sell a version without sharing its changes.
The LGPL is a weaker copyleft made for libraries. It is still a copyleft licence in the GNU family, just with fewer demands on programs that use the library.
The MIT licence lets you do almost anything, as long as the copyright notice and the licence text come along.
The AGPL extends the idea to network use: running a modified version as a web service still means sharing its source.
Apache 2.0 is a permissive licence: changes may stay proprietary, and the main duties are credit and notices.
SA means ShareAlike: adaptations must be shared under the same terms. That is copyleft for content such as Jonas’s art.
CC BY only asks you to credit the creator. Anyone may reuse and remix the work and share the result on other terms.
CC0 gives up as many rights as the law allows, so anyone can use the work without conditions.

items.text: The licence that Ada picked so that other studios may build on the Pixel Raiders engine, even in commercial games, and keep their changes private.
items.why: A licence that lets others keep their changes private is permissive. A copyleft licence would have made them share.

items.text: The licence of the Linux kernel and many GNU tools, which makes everyone who distributes the software pass on the same freedoms.
items.why: The kernel is under the GPL, a copyleft licence: modified versions that are distributed must stay free under the same terms.

items.text: The text in `/usr/share/common-licenses/GPL-3` on a Debian system.
items.why: That file holds the GNU General Public License, version 3, a copyleft licence. Debian keeps copies of the common licences there.
